_about: Derived from src/data/api-snapshot.json by scripts/build-recall-corpus.mjs. Invented sample data.

docs.title: Allow 30s of clock-skew leeway when verifying exp and nbf
docs.insight: Freshly issued tokens can look not-yet-valid to a node whose clock lags by a second or two.
docs.text:
Allow 30s of clock-skew leeway when verifying exp and nbf
Freshly issued tokens can look not-yet-valid to a node whose clock lags by a second or two.
Roughly 1 in 200 logins returned 401 on the very next request.
Verifier node clock was ~1.5s behind the issuer and nbf was set to the issue time.
Configure clockTolerance of 30 seconds and run chrony on all nodes.
Never verify time-bound claims without leeway.
JWTClaimValidationFailed: nbf claim timestamp check failed
intermittent 401 right after login
```ts
await jwtVerify(token, jwks, { clockTolerance: "30s" });
```

Check drift with `chronyc tracking`. Anything over 100 ms between nodes is worth alerting on.

docs.title: Share one HS256 secret across services for JWT verification
docs.insight: A single JWT_SECRET env var is the quickest way to verify tokens everywhere.
docs.text:
Share one HS256 secret across services for JWT verification
A single JWT_SECRET env var is the quickest way to verify tokens everywhere.
Services need to authenticate the same bearer tokens.
No shared verification mechanism.
Set the same JWT_SECRET in every service and verify with HS256.
Keep the secret in the secrets manager.
```ts
jwt.verify(token, process.env.JWT_SECRET!, { algorithms: ["HS256"] });
```

Quick to set up. Downside found later: any service that can verify can also mint tokens, and rotating the secret needs a coordinated deploy.

docs.title: Verify JWTs with RS256 and a cached JWKS endpoint
docs.insight: Sign with a private key held by the auth service; every other service verifies with public keys fetched from JWKS by kid.

docs.title: Rotate refresh tokens and revoke the family on reuse
docs.insight: Single-use refresh tokens let you detect theft: a second use of a spent token means someone copied it.
docs.text:
Rotate refresh tokens and revoke the family on reuse
Single-use refresh tokens let you detect theft: a second use of a spent token means someone copied it.
Long-lived static refresh tokens gave attackers a silent 30-day foothold.
No way to distinguish the legitimate client from a replaying attacker.
Issue a new refresh token per refresh, store a family id, revoke the whole family on reuse.
Refresh endpoints must be atomic: compare-and-swap the token hash.
```sql
UPDATE refresh_tokens
SET used_at = now()
WHERE token_hash = $1 AND used_at IS NULL AND expires_at > now()
RETURNING family_id;   -- zero rows => reuse or expiry => revoke family
```

Allow a ~10 s grace window for multi-tab races, otherwise honest users get logged out.

docs.title: SameSite=Strict cookies break the OAuth redirect back to the app
docs.insight: Cross-site top-level navigations do not send Strict cookies; Lax does for GET.
docs.text:
SameSite=Strict cookies break the OAuth redirect back to the app
Cross-site top-level navigations do not send Strict cookies; Lax does for GET.
User lands back on widgetly logged out after a successful Google login.
Session cookie was SameSite=Strict so the callback request carried no cookie.
Use SameSite=Lax for the session cookie, keep CSRF tokens for state-changing routes.
Strict is for cookies that never need to survive an inbound cross-site link.
```http
Set-Cookie: sid=...; Path=/; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax
```

Debug tip: DevTools > Application > Cookies shows a "blocked due to SameSite" reason on the callback request.

docs.title: Cache node_modules with actions/cache keyed on the lockfile
docs.insight: Restore node_modules directly when package-lock.json has not changed.
docs.text:
Cache node_modules with actions/cache keyed on the lockfile
Restore node_modules directly when package-lock.json has not changed.
npm ci dominated CI wall time.
No dependency caching configured.
actions/cache on node_modules with a hashFiles(lockfile) key.
Key the cache on the lockfile hash.
```yaml
- uses: actions/cache@v4
  with:
    path: node_modules
    key: nm-${{ hashFiles('package-lock.json') }}
```

Superseded after a Node 20 to 22 upgrade restored binaries built for the old ABI.

docs.title: Use concurrency groups to cancel superseded CI runs
docs.insight: A concurrency group per ref cancels runs that a newer push has made irrelevant, but never on main.
docs.text:
Use concurrency groups to cancel superseded CI runs
A concurrency group per ref cancels runs that a newer push has made irrelevant, but never on main.
Rapid pushes queued many identical runs and delayed required checks.
Workflows had no concurrency control.
Add concurrency with cancel-in-progress conditional on non-main refs.
Cancel PR runs, never deploy runs.
```yaml
concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.ref != 'refs/heads/main' }}
```

Saved about 35 percent of runner minutes on the widgetly repo.

docs.title: Cache ~/.npm to speed up npm ci
docs.insight: Persist the npm download cache between runs.
docs.text:
Cache ~/.npm to speed up npm ci
Persist the npm download cache between runs.
Every CI run re-downloads all tarballs.
Ephemeral runners start with an empty ~/.npm.
Cache the ~/.npm directory with actions/cache.
Use npm ci, not npm install, in CI.
```yaml
- uses: actions/cache@v4
  with:
    path: ~/.npm
    key: npm-${{ hashFiles('package-lock.json') }}
```

Saves downloads but not the extraction and link step, so gains were modest (about 25 percent).

docs.title: Cache the pnpm store with setup-node, not node_modules
docs.insight: Cache the content-addressed store and let pnpm hard-link; restores are fast and safe across Node versions.
docs.text:
Cache the pnpm store with setup-node, not node_modules
Cache the content-addressed store and let pnpm hard-link; restores are fast and safe across Node versions.
Caching node_modules produced stale native bindings after Node upgrades.
node_modules contains compiled artifacts tied to the Node ABI.
actions/setup-node with cache: pnpm, then pnpm install --frozen-lockfile.
Cache the package-manager store, never node_modules.
```yaml
- uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4
- uses: actions/setup-node@v4
  with:
    node-version: 22
    cache: pnpm
- run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
```

Install drops from 70 s cold to 9 s warm. The cache key is derived from `pnpm-lock.yaml` automatically.

docs.title: BuildKit cache mounts speed up package installs and survive layer busts
docs.insight: RUN --mount=type=cache keeps the package-manager cache outside the image so even a layer bust is fast.
docs.text:
BuildKit cache mounts speed up package installs and survive layer busts
RUN --mount=type=cache keeps the package-manager cache outside the image so even a layer bust is fast.
Lockfile changes still re-downloaded hundreds of MB of packages.
Layer cache is all-or-nothing; the package store was thrown away with the layer.
Mount a persistent cache directory for the package manager during RUN.
Use cache mounts for cargo registry, pnpm store and pip cache.
```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1.7
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cargo/registry \
    --mount=type=cache,target=/app/target \
    cargo build --release
```

On CI the mount cache is local to the runner; export it with `cache-to: type=gha,mode=max` or it is lost between jobs.

docs.title: Order Dockerfile layers: dependency manifests before source
docs.insight: Copy only package.json and the lockfile, install, then copy the source so edits do not bust the install layer.
docs.text:
Order Dockerfile layers: dependency manifests before source
Copy only package.json and the lockfile, install, then copy the source so edits do not bust the install layer.
Every commit reinstalled all dependencies in the image build.
COPY . . came before the install step, so any file change invalidated it.
Copy manifests first, install, then copy source.
Least-frequently-changing inputs go highest in the Dockerfile.
```dockerfile
FROM node:22-slim AS deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json pnpm-lock.yaml ./
RUN corepack enable && pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

FROM deps AS build
COPY . .
RUN pnpm build
```

Same rule as any language: manifests, install, then source. Pair with a `.dockerignore` that excludes `node_modules` and `.git`.

docs.title: git rebase --onto to move a stacked branch after its parent is squash-merged
docs.insight: Name the old base explicitly so only the child's own commits are replayed on top of main.
docs.text:
git rebase --onto to move a stacked branch after its parent is squash-merged
Name the old base explicitly so only the child's own commits are replayed on top of main.
Child PR re-included the parent's commits after the parent was squash-merged.
Squash creates a new commit, so git cannot see the parent commits as already upstream.
git rebase --onto main <old-parent-tip> child-branch
Record the parent tip SHA before merging it.
```bash
git fetch origin
git rebase --onto origin/main feature-parent feature-child
git push --force-with-lease
```

`--force-with-lease` refuses to overwrite commits you have not seen.

docs.title: HPA shows <unknown> targets until pods declare CPU requests
docs.insight: Utilization is a percentage of the request, so no request means no metric and no scaling.
docs.text:
HPA shows <unknown> targets until pods declare CPU requests
Utilization is a percentage of the request, so no request means no metric and no scaling.
Autoscaler never scaled the API despite 95 percent CPU.
Container spec had limits but no requests.
Set resources.requests.cpu and memory; verify with kubectl describe hpa.
Always set requests; set memory limit equal to request.
kubectl get hpa shows TARGETS <unknown>/70%
unable to compute replica count: missing request for cpu
```yaml
resources:
  requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 256Mi }
  limits:   { memory: 256Mi }
```

Memory limit above the request invites OOMKilled once the node is under pressure.

docs.title: Gate traffic with a readiness probe and a startupProbe for slow boots
docs.insight: Readiness controls traffic, liveness restarts; a startupProbe keeps liveness quiet until warmup ends.
docs.text:
Gate traffic with a readiness probe and a startupProbe for slow boots
Readiness controls traffic, liveness restarts; a startupProbe keeps liveness quiet until warmup ends.
Pods were killed while loading the sqlx pool and caches, looping forever.
Liveness probe started at 5s but the app needs ~25s.
Add startupProbe with failureThreshold 30, keep liveness lenient, readiness hits /readyz.
Liveness must never depend on downstreams like the database.
```yaml
startupProbe:  { httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 }, periodSeconds: 2, failureThreshold: 30 }
readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /readyz,  port: 8080 }, periodSeconds: 5 }
livenessProbe:  { httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 }, periodSeconds: 10 }
```

`/healthz` returns 200 if the process is up; `/readyz` also checks the DB pool.

docs.title: Collapse concurrent cache misses with singleflight to stop stampedes
docs.insight: When a hot key expires, only one caller should rebuild it; the rest wait on that result.
docs.text:
Collapse concurrent cache misses with singleflight to stop stampedes
When a hot key expires, only one caller should rebuild it; the rest wait on that result.
Expiry of the pricing cache sent 400 identical queries to PostgreSQL in the same second.
Every miss recomputed independently, no coalescing and synchronized TTLs.
In-process singleflight keyed by cache key, plus +/-10 percent TTL jitter.
Jitter every TTL; coalesce every expensive miss.
```rust
let price = flights
    .work(&key, || async { load_price_from_pg(&pool, sku).await })
    .await?;
redis.set_ex(&key, &price, 300 + rand::random::<u64>() % 60).await?;
```

Across replicas you still get one rebuild per replica; for global coalescing take a short `SET NX PX` lock.

docs.title: Use EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) before adding an index
docs.insight: Buffer counts and actual row estimates, not cost numbers, tell you whether an index will help.
docs.text:
Use EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) before adding an index
Buffer counts and actual row estimates, not cost numbers, tell you whether an index will help.
Indexes were added on guesswork and a few made writes slower without helping reads.
Planner estimates were stale; nobody compared estimated to actual rows.
Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) and ANALYZE the table first.
Capture the plan before and after; paste both in the PR.
```sql
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;
```

Look for `rows=` vs `actual rows=` differing by 10x, and `Buffers: shared read` being large.
If estimates are off, `ANALYZE orders;` and re-run before touching the schema.

docs.title: Set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout to stop lock leaks
docs.insight: A request that opens a transaction and then crashes or awaits an HTTP call keeps its locks until the session dies.
docs.text:
Set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout to stop lock leaks
A request that opens a transaction and then crashes or awaits an HTTP call keeps its locks until the session dies.
A migration blocked behind an abandoned transaction for 40 minutes.
Handler held a transaction open across an outbound HTTP call that never returned.
Set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '30s' and move HTTP calls outside the transaction.
Never await network I/O while holding a transaction.
## Diagnosis

```sql
SELECT pid, now() - xact_start AS age, query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state = 'idle in transaction'
ORDER BY age DESC;
```

## Fix

```sql
ALTER ROLE acme_app SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '30s';
```

docs.title: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a migration transaction
docs.insight: Tell the migration runner to skip its wrapping transaction for that one file.
docs.text:
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a migration transaction
Tell the migration runner to skip its wrapping transaction for that one file.
Index migration fails on apply while the same SQL works in psql.
sqlx wraps every migration file in BEGIN/COMMIT by default.
Add the `-- no-transaction` directive on the first line of the migration.
One CONCURRENTLY statement per migration file, nothing else.
ERROR: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block
## Solution

```sql
-- no-transaction
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS idx_orders_customer_id
    ON orders (customer_id);
```

If the build is interrupted it leaves an INVALID index; drop it before retrying:
`DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_customer_id;`

docs.title: Raise Postgres max_connections to fix pool timeouts
docs.insight: Bumping max_connections to 500 relieved pool timeouts at first.
docs.text:
Raise Postgres max_connections to fix pool timeouts
Bumping max_connections to 500 relieved pool timeouts at first.
API returns 503s when the pool is exhausted.
Database cap too low for peak concurrency.
Set max_connections = 500 in postgresql.conf and restart.
Raise max_connections when clients are refused.
## Solution

```sql
ALTER SYSTEM SET max_connections = 500;
-- restart required
```

Worked for two weeks. Memory use per backend (~10 MB) then caused OOM kills on the 4 GB instance.

docs.title: asyncio.gather swallows sibling failures unless return_exceptions is set
docs.insight: By default gather raises the first exception and leaves the rest running; use TaskGroup for structured cancellation.
docs.text:
asyncio.gather swallows sibling failures unless return_exceptions is set
By default gather raises the first exception and leaves the rest running; use TaskGroup for structured cancellation.
A failed fetch left orphaned tasks writing partial files.
gather does not cancel siblings on error.
Use asyncio.TaskGroup (3.11+) or gather(return_exceptions=True) and inspect results.
Prefer TaskGroup; gather only when you handle every result.
```python
async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
    tasks = [tg.create_task(fetch(u)) for u in urls]
# any failure cancels the others and raises ExceptionGroup
results = [t.result() for t in tasks]
```

docs.title: Guard async effect results with an ignore flag in cleanup
docs.insight: A local `ignore` boolean set in the cleanup stops late responses from calling setState.

docs.title: Abort stale fetches in useEffect to avoid out-of-order results
docs.insight: Responses can arrive out of order; cancel the previous request when the dependency changes.

docs.title: useEffect runs twice in dev StrictMode; make effects idempotent
docs.insight: StrictMode mounts, unmounts and remounts to flush out missing cleanup; do not suppress it, fix the effect.

docs.title: axum: body-consuming extractor must be the last argument
docs.insight: Json, Form and Bytes consume the request body, so axum only allows one and only in last position.
docs.text:
axum: body-consuming extractor must be the last argument
Json, Form and Bytes consume the request body, so axum only allows one and only in last position.
Handler refuses to compile with an unhelpful Handler trait error.
FromRequest (body) extractors are ordered after FromRequestParts extractors.
Move Json<T> to the final parameter; add #[axum::debug_handler] to get a readable error.
Put State, Path, Query first; Json or Form last.
the trait bound `fn(Json<T>, State<S>): Handler` is not satisfied
## Problem

```text
error[E0277]: the trait bound `fn(Json<NewUser>, State<AppState>) -> ... : Handler<_, _>` is not satisfied
```

## Solution

```rust
#[axum::debug_handler]
async fn create_user(
    State(app): State<AppState>,
    Json(body): Json<NewUser>,   // body extractor LAST
) -> Result<StatusCode, ApiError> { /* ... */ }
```

`debug_handler` turns the trait soup into "Json<_> must be the last argument".

docs.title: cargo-chef keeps Rust dependency layers cached in Docker
docs.insight: Plan dependencies with cargo chef prepare so the compile layer only invalidates when Cargo.lock changes.
docs.text:
cargo-chef keeps Rust dependency layers cached in Docker
Plan dependencies with cargo chef prepare so the compile layer only invalidates when Cargo.lock changes.
Any source edit invalidated the cargo build layer and recompiled 300 crates.
COPY . . before cargo build placed source above the dependency compile step.
Three-stage Dockerfile: chef prepare, chef cook, then build the app.
Dependencies first, source last, in every language.
## Solution

```dockerfile
FROM lukemathwalker/cargo-chef:latest-rust-1.83 AS chef
WORKDIR /app

FROM chef AS planner
COPY . .
RUN cargo chef prepare --recipe-path recipe.json

FROM chef AS builder
COPY --from=planner /app/recipe.json recipe.json
RUN cargo chef cook --release --recipe-path recipe.json   # cached layer
COPY . .
RUN cargo build --release --bin acme-api
```

Cold build: 14 min. Warm build after a source-only change: 90 s.

docs.title: Size the sqlx pool from PgBouncer limits, not from load
docs.insight: Total connections = replicas x max_connections must stay under PgBouncer default_pool_size; extra connections only queue.
docs.text:
Size the sqlx pool from PgBouncer limits, not from load
Total connections = replicas x max_connections must stay under PgBouncer default_pool_size; extra connections only queue.
PoolTimedOut errors under load even after raising max_connections.
Eight replicas x 50 connections exceeded the PgBouncer pool of 100, so most sat waiting.
PgPoolOptions::max_connections(10) per replica, transaction pooling mode, statement cache off.
Pool size is a budget shared across replicas, not a per-pod dial.
PoolTimedOut after 30s
FATAL: sorry, too many clients already
## Problem

`PoolTimedOut` at p99 even after bumping `max_connections` to 50.

## Solution

```rust
let pool = PgPoolOptions::new()
    .max_connections(10)                 // 8 replicas x 10 = 80 < 100
    .acquire_timeout(Duration::from_secs(3))
    .connect(&url).await?;
```

PgBouncer in `pool_mode = transaction`; with it, disable prepared-statement caching:
`PgConnectOptions::statement_cache_capacity(0)`.

## Context

Replaces the earlier "raise Postgres max_connections" advice, which only moved the queue into the database.

docs.title: sqlx query! macros need SQLX_OFFLINE in CI
docs.insight: Commit .sqlx/ query metadata and build with SQLX_OFFLINE=true so CI never needs a live database.
docs.text:
sqlx query! macros need SQLX_OFFLINE in CI
Commit .sqlx/ query metadata and build with SQLX_OFFLINE=true so CI never needs a live database.
cargo build passes locally but fails on GitHub Actions at the first query! macro.
sqlx query! checks SQL against DATABASE_URL at compile time and CI has no database.
Run cargo sqlx prepare locally, commit .sqlx/, set SQLX_OFFLINE=true in the workflow.
Always re-run cargo sqlx prepare after touching any query! string.
error: error communicating with database: Connection refused
cargo build fails in CI only
## Problem

`cargo build` is green locally and red in CI with `error communicating with database`.
The `query!` family of macros connects to `DATABASE_URL` at compile time.

## Solution

```bash
cargo sqlx prepare --workspace   # writes .sqlx/query-*.json
git add .sqlx
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
env:
  SQLX_OFFLINE: "true"
```

## Anti-Pattern

Spinning up a Postgres service container only to satisfy the compiler. It works, but doubles CI time and hides stale metadata.
Add `cargo sqlx prepare --check` as a CI step so stale `.sqlx/` fails the build.

docs.title: Run argon2 hashing inside spawn_blocking
docs.insight: CPU-bound work on a tokio worker thread starves every other task on that thread.
docs.text:
Run argon2 hashing inside spawn_blocking
CPU-bound work on a tokio worker thread starves every other task on that thread.
Login bursts froze unrelated endpoints, including /healthz.
argon2 verify takes ~80ms of pure CPU and was awaited directly on the async worker.
Wrap hash and verify in tokio::task::spawn_blocking.
Anything over ~1ms of CPU goes to spawn_blocking or a rayon pool.
## Problem

`/login` bursts caused `/healthz` to time out. Flamegraph showed the worker threads parked inside `argon2::verify`.

## Solution

```rust
let ok = tokio::task::spawn_blocking(move || {
    argon2.verify_password(pw.as_bytes(), &parsed_hash).is_ok()
})
.await?;
```

Size the blocking pool with `Builder::max_blocking_threads` if login volume is high.

## Anti-Pattern

Calling the sync verify inside an `async fn` and trusting `.await` elsewhere to yield. It never yields mid-hash.

docs.title: Flaky e2e: waitForLoadState('networkidle') hangs on polling pages
docs.insight: networkidle never fires when the page polls or holds a websocket; wait for a concrete element instead.
docs.text:
Flaky e2e: waitForLoadState('networkidle') hangs on polling pages
networkidle never fires when the page polls or holds a websocket; wait for a concrete element instead.
Dashboard test hung until timeout because the page polls /metrics every 5 seconds.
networkidle requires 500 ms with no requests, which polling prevents.
Wait for a locator that proves the data rendered.
Avoid networkidle; Playwright docs discourage it too.
page.waitForLoadState: Timeout 30000ms exceeded
dashboard test only fails on CI
```ts
// hangs
await page.goto("/dashboard", { waitUntil: "networkidle" });
// stable
await page.goto("/dashboard");
await expect(page.getByTestId("kpi-revenue")).toHaveText(/\$\d/);
```

Rule of thumb: if the page has polling, SSE or a websocket, there is no idle moment to wait for.
Prefer a web-first assertion on the element that proves the data arrived.

docs.title: Playwright: rely on auto-waiting locators, never waitForTimeout
docs.insight: Web-first assertions retry until the condition holds; fixed sleeps either waste time or flake.

docs.title: pytest: create the database once per session, roll back per test
docs.insight: Session-scoped engine plus a per-test transaction that is rolled back gives isolation at a fraction of the cost.
docs.text:
pytest: create the database once per session, roll back per test
Session-scoped engine plus a per-test transaction that is rolled back gives isolation at a fraction of the cost.
Creating a fresh schema per test made 600 tests crawl.
Function-scoped fixture ran migrations every time.
scope='session' for the engine, function-scoped connection with an outer transaction and rollback.
Isolation by rollback, not by recreating the world.
```python
@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def engine():
    eng = create_engine(TEST_URL)
    run_migrations(eng)          # once
    yield eng

@pytest.fixture
def db(engine):
    with engine.connect() as conn, conn.begin() as tx:
        yield conn
        tx.rollback()
```

Suite time: 4 min 10 s down to 38 s.

docs.title: Use `satisfies` to check an object literal without widening its type
docs.insight: `: Record<string, Route>` loses key literals; `satisfies` keeps them while still validating shape.
docs.text:
Use `satisfies` to check an object literal without widening its type
`: Record<string, Route>` loses key literals; `satisfies` keeps them while still validating shape.
Route table lost its literal keys, so typos in route names compiled fine.
Type annotation widens the inferred type to the annotation.
Replace the annotation with `satisfies Record<string, Route>`.
Annotate function boundaries, satisfy object literals.
```ts
const routes = {
  home: { path: "/", auth: false },
  billing: { path: "/billing", auth: true },
} satisfies Record<string, Route>;

routes.billing.path;   // "/billing" (literal), typos on keys now error
```
